title: Des Herrn und des Teufels Gethier
titleEn: The Lord's Animals and the Devil's
part: The Lord's Animals and the Devil's
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 148. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (Thiere, erschaffen, giengen, ließ).
about: KHM 148 is an origin story told as a contest: God creates the wolves as his own hounds and, noticing he has forgotten the goat, the Devil steps in and makes goats with long tails that snag constantly in the thornbrakes. Each side keeps meddling with the other's creatures — the wolves set loose on the goats, the Devil retaliating in kind — until the tale settles, in its last line, why goats to this day have devil's eyes and bitten-off tails. It is a short, dry etiological joke rather than an adventure.

sentences.t: Gott der Herr hatte alle Thiere erschaffen und sich die Wölfe zu seinen Hunden auserwählet: blos der Geis hatte er vergessen.
sentences.l: God the Lord had all animals created and to himself the wolves as his hounds chosen out: only the goat had he forgotten.
sentences.i: God the Lord had created all the animals and had chosen the wolves for his hounds — only the goat he had forgotten.
sentences.n: “Thiere” and “blos” are the 1857 spellings of Tiere and bloß. “auserwählet” is an older full form of auserwählt. In “der Geis hatte er vergessen”, “der Geis” is most likely the genitive of the feminine die Geiß (older Geis): vergessen once governed the genitive, where modern German takes an accusative. Others read it as an older feminine form simply standing where we would expect the accusative; the sense is the same either way.

sentences.t: Da richtete sich der Teufel an, wollte auch schaffen und machte die Geise mit feinen langen Schwänzen.
sentences.l: Then set the devil himself to it, wanted also to create, and made the goats with fine long tails.
sentences.i: Then the Devil set himself to it: he wanted to create as well, and he made the goats with fine long tails.
sentences.n: “sich anrichten” here has its older sense, ‘to set oneself to a thing’; modern anrichten means to serve up a dish or to cause damage. It is separable, and the halves stand apart: “richtete … an”.

sentences.t: Wenn sie nun zur Weide giengen, blieben sie gewöhnlich mit ihren Schwänzen in den Dornhecken hängen,
sentences.l: When they now to the pasture went, remained they usually with their tails in the thorn-hedges hanging,
sentences.i: Now when they went out to pasture, they would usually be left hanging by their tails in the thorn hedges,
sentences.n: “hängen bleiben” — to be caught, to get stuck — is separable, and the two halves stand far apart here: “blieben … hängen”. “giengen” is the 1857 spelling of gingen.

sentences.t: da mußte der Teufel hineingehen und sie mit vieler Mühe losknüpfen.
sentences.l: there had the devil to go in and them with much trouble to untie.
sentences.i: and the Devil had to go in and work them loose with a great deal of trouble.
sentences.n: “losknüpfen” is literally to un-knot: he picks the snagged tails out of the thorns.

sentences.t: Das verdroß ihn zuletzt, war her und biß jeder Geis den Schwanz ab, wie noch heut des Tags an den Stümpfen zu sehen ist.
sentences.l: That vexed him at last, [he] was at it and bit off from each goat the tail, as still to this day at the stumps to be seen is.
sentences.i: In the end it vexed him, and he went at them and bit the tail off every goat, as may still be seen today from the stumps.
sentences.n: The subject of the second and third verbs is gapped in the German (“Das verdroß ihn zuletzt, war her und biß…”); [he] is supplied in square brackets. “war her” is an old turn — went at it, set upon them. “biß jeder Geis den Schwanz ab” is the dative of possession: bit the tail off each goat. “heut des Tags” is an old genitive of time.

sentences.t: Nun ließ er sie zwar allein weiden,
sentences.l: Now let he them indeed alone graze,
sentences.i: Now he did let them graze by themselves,
sentences.n: “zwar” concedes a point that the following clause will overturn: he did let them graze — but.

sentences.t: aber es geschah, daß Gott der Herr zusah wie sie bald einen fruchtbaren Baum benagten, bald die edeln Reben beschädigten, bald andere zarte Pflanzen verderbten.
sentences.l: but it happened that God the Lord looked on how they now a fruit-bearing tree gnawed, now the noble vines damaged, now other tender plants ruined.
sentences.i: but it came to pass that God the Lord saw how they would gnaw a fruit tree here, damage the noble vines there, and spoil other tender plants.
sentences.n: “bald … bald … bald …” means ‘now this, now that’, one thing after another. “edeln” is an older inflection of edlen. The vine matters: goat and vine are old enemies, and the tale ends by guarding it.

sentences.t: Das jammerte ihn, so daß er aus Güte und Gnaden seine Wölfe dran hetzte, welche die Geise, die da giengen, bald zerrissen.
sentences.l: That grieved him, so that he out of goodness and grace his wolves at them set, which the goats, that went there, soon tore to pieces.
sentences.i: That grieved him, so that out of kindness and mercy he set his wolves on them, and they soon tore to pieces the goats that were out there.
sentences.n: “jammern” with an accusative object — “das jammerte ihn” — means it moved him to pity. “dran” is the spoken short form of daran, and “hetzen an” is to set a hound on something. Here “bald” means soon, not the ‘now … now …’ of the sentence before.

sentences.t: Wie der Teufel das vernahm, trat er vor den Herrn und sprach „dein Geschöpf hat mir das meine zerrissen.“
sentences.l: As the devil that heard, stepped he before the Lord and spoke “your creature has to me the mine torn to pieces.”
sentences.i: When the Devil heard of it, he stepped before the Lord and said, “Your creature has torn mine to pieces.”
sentences.n: “wie” here is temporal, ‘when’. “das meine” = what is mine; the dative “mir” marks the one who suffers the loss — a construction English turns into a possessive.

sentences.t: Der Herr antwortete „was hattest du es zu Schaden erschaffen!“
sentences.l: The Lord answered “why had you it to harm created!”
sentences.i: The Lord answered, “Why did you create it for harm!”
sentences.n: “was” does duty for warum, ‘why’, in the older language, and the exclamation mark makes it a reproach rather than a question. “zu Schaden erschaffen” — made so as to do damage.

sentences.t: Der Teufel sagte „ich mußte das: gleichwie selbst mein Sinn auf Schaden geht, konnte was ich erschaffen keine andere Natur haben, und mußt mirs theuer zahlen.“
sentences.l: The devil said “I had to [do] that: just as my own mind goes toward harm, could what I create no other nature have, and [you] must pay me for it dearly.”
sentences.i: The Devil said, “I had no choice: since my own bent is toward harm, what I create could have no other nature — and you must pay me dearly for it.”
sentences.n: Two supplies in square brackets: the verb of “ich mußte das” is elided, and the subject of “mußt mirs theuer zahlen” is gapped. “gleichwie” = just as; “mirs” = mir es; “theuer” is the 1857 spelling of teuer.

sentences.t: „Ich zahl dirs sobald das Eichenlaub abfällt, dann komm, dein Geld ist schon gezählt.“
sentences.l: “I pay you for it as soon as the oak-leaves fall off, then come, your money is already counted.”
sentences.i: “I will pay you as soon as the oak leaves fall; then come — your money is counted out already.”
sentences.n: The Lord answers with no speech tag at all; the change of speaker is left to the quotation marks. “dirs” = dir es, and the present tense “ich zahl” carries the future. “abfallen” is separable: “fällt … ab”. The promise is a trap, as the next sentences show.

sentences.t: Als das Eichenlaub abgefallen war, kam der Teufel und forderte seine Schuld.
sentences.l: When the oak-leaves fallen off were, came the devil and demanded his debt.
sentences.i: When the oak leaves had fallen, the Devil came and demanded what was owed him.
sentences.n: “seine Schuld” is the debt owed to him, not a guilt of his own; Schuld carries both senses, and money is meant here.

sentences.t: Der Herr aber sprach „in der Kirche zu Constantinopel steht eine hohe Eiche, die hat noch alles ihr Laub.“
sentences.l: The Lord however spoke “in the church at Constantinople stands a high oak, it has still all its leaves.”
sentences.i: But the Lord said, “In the church at Constantinople there stands a tall oak, and it still has all its leaves.”
sentences.n: “zu” with a place name is the older ‘at’ (as in Frankfurt am Main). “die” opening the second clause is a demonstrative picking up “Eiche” — it works as ‘and that one’.

sentences.t: Mit Toben und Fluchen entwich der Teufel und wollte die Eiche suchen, irrte sechs Monate in der Wüstenei, ehe er sie befand,
sentences.l: With raging and cursing slipped the devil away and wanted the oak to seek, strayed six months in the wilderness before he it found,
sentences.i: Raging and cursing, the Devil made off to look for the oak, and strayed six months in the wilderness before he found it,
sentences.n: “die Wüstenei” is an old word for a waste, a desolate country. “befinden” keeps its old sense ‘to find, come upon’, quite unlike the modern sich befinden, to be situated.

sentences.t: und als er wieder kam, waren derweil wieder alle andere Eichen voll grüner Blätter.
sentences.l: and when he again came, were meanwhile again all other oaks full of green leaves.
sentences.i: and when he came back, all the other oaks were meanwhile full of green leaves again.
sentences.n: “derweil” = meanwhile. “alle andere Eichen” keeps an older inflection where modern German has alle anderen Eichen. “voll” takes the genitive: “voll grüner Blätter”.

sentences.t: Da mußte er seine Schuld fahren lassen, stach im Zorn allen übrigen Geisen die Augen aus und setzte ihnen seine eigenen ein.
sentences.l: Then had he his debt to let go, put out in anger to all the remaining goats the eyes and set in to them his own.
sentences.i: So he had to let his claim go; in his anger he put out the eyes of all the goats that were left and set his own in their place.
sentences.n: “fahren lassen” = to let go, give up. The dative of possession twice over: “stach allen übrigen Geisen die Augen aus”, “setzte ihnen seine eigenen ein” — the eyes belong to the goats. Both verbs are separable: “stach … aus”, “setzte … ein”.

sentences.t: Darum haben alle Geise Teufelsaugen und abgebissene Schwänze, und er nimmt gern ihre Gestalt an.
sentences.l: Therefore have all goats devil's-eyes and bitten-off tails, and he takes gladly their shape on.
sentences.i: That is why all goats have the Devil’s eyes and bitten-off tails, and why he is glad to take their shape.
sentences.n: The closing etiology: the tale exists to account for the goat’s strange slit eye and its stump of a tail. “annehmen” is separable — “nimmt … an” — and “gern” with a verb means to do a thing willingly, to like doing it.

glossary.befand: befinden — to find, come upon (3rd sg. past; the modern sich befinden means to be situated)
glossary.jammerte: jammern — to move to pity, grieve (3rd sg. past with an accusative object: das jammerte ihn; also to lament)
glossary.richtete: sich anrichten — to set oneself to a thing (3rd sg. past richtete … an; sich in die Höhe richten is to straighten up)
glossary.schaffen: schaffen — to create, bring into being (infinitive; the other schaffen means to manage, to get a thing done)
glossary.schuld: die Schuld — debt, what is owed (also fault, guilt)
glossary.setzte: einsetzen — to set in, put in (3rd sg. past setzte … ein; separable; setzen alone is to set, to put)
glossary.stach: ausstechen — to put out (an eye) (3rd sg. past stach … aus; separable; stechen alone is to pierce, to stab)
glossary.zahl: zahlen — to pay (1st sg. pres. with the -e dropped: ich zahl)
glossary.zerrissen: zerreißen — to tear to pieces (3rd pl. past and past participle)
